passage:
Day one, three weeks before boards: Rajni made a timetable with every subject crammed in, but on the first evening she spent forty minutes answering messages. She went to bed feeling sick and behind.

Day ten: Her friend Tejas showed her his trick: phone in the kitchen, twenty-five minutes of work, five minutes of walking around. Rajni tried it with chemistry. It was hard to sit still for the first two blocks, and she almost went for her phone. By the fourth, she had finished a whole chapter of questions.

The morning of the exam: Her hands were cold. She breathed slowly, read all the questions first, and started with the ones she knew. She finished with ten minutes to check.

qa.q: Where did Tejas keep his phone while studying?
qa.a: He kept his phone in the kitchen.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel after the first evening of her timetable?
qa.a: She felt sick and behind, since forty minutes of messages had eaten her study time and made her doubt her plan.

qa.q: Which part of Rajni's exam morning approach worked, and why?
qa.a: Reading all the questions first and starting with ones she knew calmed her nerves and saved time, so she had ten minutes left to check.

qa.q: How might Tejas feel seeing Rajni use his trick?
qa.a: He might feel glad and a bit proud that his simple method helped a friend, and it may make them study partners.

grounding: It shows a teen moving over weeks from a crammed, distracted plan to focused revision and a calm exam strategy.

passage: Beta, when your Sonali Didi was in Class 12, she panicked like you are now. I was her tuition teacher, remember? Lokesh, sit, listen. Two months before the exam she came to me with ten textbooks and cried that she could not finish. I asked her to close them all and write on one page what she already knew for each chapter. The page with the fewest lines, that was where she started. She read for one hour, then tested herself without the book. She hated it; she said it felt like failing all day. But her marks in the practice papers went up steadily. On exam day she told me, "Sir, I wasn't calm, but I knew what I knew." That is what I want for you too.

qa.q: What did Sonali write on one page for each chapter?
qa.a: She wrote what she already knew for each chapter.

qa.q: Why did Sonali hate testing herself without the book?
qa.a: It felt like failing all day, because it showed her the gaps in her memory, which was uncomfortable even though it helped.

qa.q: What could Lokesh try from Sonali's story when planning his own revision?
qa.a: He could list what he knows for each chapter, start with the weakest one, and test himself instead of just rereading.

qa.q: How does the teacher seem to see Lokesh's panic?
qa.a: He sees it as normal and familiar, like Sonali's, and hopes Lokesh can feel the same quiet confidence even if he is not calm.

grounding: An elder teacher tells a younger student how a past pupil planned revision and handled a high-stakes exam.

passage: Reena had one week until her maths exam, and the builders next door had started drilling. Her small flat had no quiet corner. Her little sister Nandini practised the harmonium in the evenings. Reena snapped at her twice and then felt awful. On Tuesday she changed the plan. She went to the library before school opened, when it was empty, and did her hardest topics then. After school, with the drilling at its worst, she did easy revision: formula cards on the balcony, earplugs from her father's toolbox. She asked Nandini to practise at seven instead of six. Nandini sulked but agreed. On Sunday night, Reena did a full paper under time. She got stuck on one question and moved on.

qa.q: When did Reena go to the library to study?
qa.a: She went before school opened, when it was empty.

qa.q: What did Reena feel after snapping at Nandini?
qa.a: She felt awful, which shows she knew the stress of the noise was making her unfair to her sister.

qa.q: What was wise about how Reena split her study time?
qa.a: She matched her hardest topics to the quiet morning and saved easy formula cards for the noisy afternoon, instead of fighting the noise.

qa.q: What is it like for Nandini to move her practice time?
qa.a: She loses her usual time and sulks, but agreeing to seven shows she is willing to help her sister, even if it costs her something.

grounding: It shows a teen planning revision around noise and time pressure and practising a timed paper before the exam.

passage: Three weeks before his Class 12 boards, Vikas stuck a timetable above his desk in their small Nagpur flat: physics in the mornings, chemistry after lunch, maths problems at night, and every Sunday afternoon a full mock paper with a timer. The hardest part wasn't the syllabus. It was his phone. Every buzz pulled him out of a derivation. So he started leaving it on the kitchen shelf with Aai while he studied, fifty minutes at a time, then a ten-minute break on the balcony. When Deepak called to go for chai at nine, Vikas hesitated. 'Saturday, after the mock,' he said. On the day of the physics paper his hands shook, so he did what he'd practised: read the whole paper, circled the easy questions and started there.

qa.q: Where did Vikas leave his phone while studying?
qa.a: On the kitchen shelf with Aai.

qa.q: What might Vikas have been feeling when Deepak called?
qa.a: He was tempted to go and a bit torn, since he wanted to see his friend but also wanted to protect his study time.

qa.q: Which part of Vikas's exam strategy could help a nervous student most?
qa.a: Reading the whole paper first and starting with the easy questions, which builds calm and momentum.

qa.q: How might Deepak see the delayed chai plan?
qa.a: Deepak might be disappointed at first but likely understands and respects Vikas's focus before boards.

grounding: Shows a teenager planning revision, resisting distraction and using a strategy in a high-stakes exam.

passage: 'Minakshi, it's eleven. Why are all the chemistry books open at once?' Bhavna mausi stood at the door. 'Because the exam is tomorrow and I don't know anything!' 'You studied all week.' 'But I keep forgetting organic.' Mausi sat on the bed. 'Okay. What's the paper pattern?' 'Three sections. Forty-five minutes each, roughly.' 'Which section is your strongest?' 'Physical chem. Numericals.' 'So start there tomorrow?' Minakshi blinked. 'I always go in order.' 'Who said you have to?' 'Nobody, I guess.' 'And tonight?' 'Just the organic reactions list. Once. Then sleep.' 'Phone?' Minakshi sighed and handed it over. 'Take it. And maybe a hug?' Mausi laughed and gave her one.

qa.q: Which section of chemistry did Minakshi say was her strongest?
qa.a: Physical chemistry, the numericals.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling when all her books were open at once?
qa.a: She was panicking and overwhelmed, fearing she didn't know anything before the exam.

qa.q: How did Mausi help Minakshi build an exam strategy?
qa.a: She asked questions that led Minakshi to start with her strongest section and to do one light revision before sleeping.

qa.q: What would change if Mausi had told Minakshi to stay up all night revising?
qa.a: Minakshi would likely be more exhausted and anxious in the exam and remember less.

grounding: Shows a teenager calming exam panic, planning final revision and choosing a strategy for a high-stakes test.

passage:
I thought I could study for the boards the way I did in Class 9: open the book, open my phone, and hope. I'm Anirban.
By January, I'd read the physics chapter four times and still couldn't solve the numericals. Kamal kept messaging memes every ten minutes, and I kept answering.
So I changed things. I made a timetable on the wall: two-hour blocks, with the hardest subject in the morning. My phone went into my father's drawer during each block. I told Kamal I'd reply at eight. He sent an angry face, then said, “Fair.”
I did past papers every Sunday, timed, like the real exam. My scores went up slowly.
On exam day, when the paper looked hard, I didn't panic. I'd seen hard papers before.

qa.q: Where did Anirban's phone go during each study block?
qa.a: Into the father's drawer.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel on exam day when the paper looked hard?
qa.a: Anirban felt calm and prepared rather than panicked, having seen hard papers before.

qa.q: Which change in Anirban's routine helped most, and why?
qa.a: Timed past papers every Sunday, because they built familiarity and calm for the real exam.

qa.q: How did Kamal react to Anirban's new rule about replying at eight?
qa.a: He sent an angry face at first, then accepted it as fair.

grounding: A teenager plans revision, blocks distraction and handles a high-stakes exam calmly.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 11. Vasudha Iyer.
In last week's mock exam, Karthik (sixteen) froze. He spent forty minutes on the first question, didn't finish, and left half the paper blank. He came to see me looking pale and said, “I know this stuff. I just panic.”
We worked out a plan together. First ten minutes: read the whole paper and mark easy, medium, hard. Start with the easy ones to build confidence. Set a rough time for each section. If stuck for more than a few minutes, move on and come back.
He practised it on two past papers. In today's second mock he finished with time to spare and scored much better.
Next step: follow-up before the board exams in March.

qa.q: How long did Karthik spend on the first question?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: How was Karthik feeling when he came to see the counsellor?
qa.a: He was anxious and frustrated, pale and saying he panics.

qa.q: Why did the exam plan help Karthik?
qa.a: It gave him a clear order and time limits, so he didn't get stuck and could build confidence.

qa.q: How might Karthik's parents feel hearing about the second mock?
qa.a: They may feel relieved and proud that he has found a way to manage exams.

grounding: A counsellor helps a sixteen-year-old plan exam strategy to handle panic.

passage:
Wednesday night
Study group today at Karthik's. We tried something new. Thirty minutes of work, phones face down in a basket, then five minutes' break. Repeat.
First block: I kept glancing at the basket like it was calling me. By the third block I forgot it was there. We finished two whole chapters of chemistry.
Karthik made us each explain one reaction to the others, without notes. I got the second one wrong and felt stupid, but now I'll never forget it.
Exams in three weeks. I'm scared, obviously. But for the first time, I have a plan, not just a panic.
— Sabina

qa.q: Where did they put their phones?
qa.a: Face down in a basket.

qa.q: How does Sabina feel about the exams now?
qa.a: Sabina feels scared but more confident and hopeful, with a plan instead of panic.

qa.q: What study habits helped the group focus?
qa.a: Thirty-minute blocks with phones away, short breaks, and explaining topics to each other.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel about the study group's success?
qa.a: Karthik probably feels pleased and proud that the method helped everyone.

grounding: A teenager learns to resist distraction and plan revision in a study group.

passage:
The board exams were three weeks away, and the power in the kasba went off every evening at seven.
Leela sat on the steps with her books while the light lasted. She'd made a chart on the wall: maths in the morning, science after school, revision of old papers at night by the solar lamp.
Her friend Vidya came with her phone. "Watch this funny reel first."
Leela hesitated. Then she shook her head. "After eight. I've got two old papers to finish."
Vidya shrugged and sat down to study too.
On exam day, Leela started with the questions she knew, then went back to the hard ones. She finished with ten minutes to spare.

qa.q: What time did the power go off every evening?
qa.a: At seven.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling when she hesitated over the reel?
qa.a: Leela felt tempted but stayed determined to finish her work.

qa.q: Which exam strategy helped Leela finish on time?
qa.a: She started with the questions she knew and went back to the hard ones later.

qa.q: How might Vidya be affected by Leela's choice?
qa.a: Vidya ends up studying too, so Leela's focus helps her friend as well.

grounding: A teen in a small town plans revision and handles exam time despite power cuts and distraction.

passage:
In Porto, three days before the national exam, Beatriz was re-reading her maths notes for the fifth time. She felt she knew nothing.
Her friend Ines came over with a folder. "Stop reading. Do these."
"Past papers? I'm not ready."
"You'll never feel ready. Time yourself."
Beatriz did one paper. She got stuck on question four and wasted twenty minutes.
"That's the lesson," said Ines. "If you're stuck, skip, come back later."
The next day, Beatriz did two more, skipping and returning. On exam day, when question three looked impossible, she took a breath, moved on, and came back to it at the end. She solved it.

qa.q: How many minutes did Beatriz waste on question four?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Beatriz feeling when she said she wasn't ready?
qa.a: Beatriz felt anxious and unsure, believing she knew nothing.

qa.q: What did Ines teach Beatriz that helped on exam day?
qa.a: Practising timed past papers and skipping hard questions to return later.

qa.q: How does Ines see Beatriz's fear of not being ready?
qa.a: Ines thinks nobody ever feels ready and that practice is better than more re-reading.

grounding: A teen in Portugal learns timed practice and skip-and-return strategy for a high-stakes exam.

passage:
Three weeks before the board exams, the hostel study hall at night sounded like a railway station: whispers, phones buzzing, someone's snack packet. Anjali had made a revision chart: one subject per evening block, the hardest topics first, when she was freshest.
Karthik sat next to her and kept showing her videos. "Just one, it's funny."
She laughed once, then lost twenty minutes. The next night she moved to the corner desk by the wall and left her phone in her locker, telling Karthik, "Ask me at ten, not before."
In the chemistry mock, she hit a question she couldn't do. Her heart started racing. She remembered her plan: circle it, move on, come back. She finished the rest, returned, and got half of it.
Karthik copied her chart the next week.

qa.q: Where did Anjali leave her phone the next night?
qa.a: She left her phone in her locker and moved to the corner desk by the wall.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling when she hit the question she couldn't do?
qa.a: Anjali felt a rush of panic, with her heart racing, but her plan helped her stay steady.

qa.q: What could Karthik take from Anjali's approach?
qa.a: Karthik could plan hard topics for fresh hours, keep the phone away during study blocks, and skip and return to stuck questions in exams.

qa.q: How might Karthik see Anjali moving to another desk?
qa.a: Karthik might feel a bit rejected at first, but later seems to see it as smart, since Karthik copies her chart.

grounding: Shows a teenager planning revision, resisting distraction and using a strategy to handle exam-room panic.

passage:
So you want to know how I survived the entrance exam? Honestly, Sharmila, it wasn't the studying. It was the ten minutes before.
I'm Gurleen, I'd done all the mocks. But in the waiting hall, a boy next to me was saying, "Did you do the rotation chapter? It's definitely coming." I hadn't revised it properly. My stomach just dropped.
I went to the washroom and splashed water on my face. And I told myself: you've done this paper forty times at home. Same format. Same clock. The strategy is the same: easy ones first, mark the hard ones, don't sit on one question more than a few minutes.
And yes, the rotation question came. I skipped it, finished the others, came back with fifteen minutes left. Got half marks. I cleared the cut-off anyway. So stay away from people revising loudly in the waiting hall, that's my whole advice.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do in the washroom?
qa.a: Gurleen splashed water on the face and remembered having done the paper forty times at home.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen's stomach drop in the waiting hall?
qa.a: Gurleen felt a sudden panic because the boy said the rotation chapter was coming and it hadn't been revised properly.

qa.q: What could Sharmila take from this before sitting a big exam?
qa.a: Sharmila could plan to avoid last-minute chatter, stick to the easy-first strategy and return to hard questions later.

qa.q: How might the boy in the waiting hall have been feeling?
qa.a: The boy was probably anxious himself, and talking loudly about topics may have been his way of calming his own nerves.

grounding: Shows a teen describing how a planned exam strategy helped Gurleen handle high-stakes panic.

passage:
I'm Pranav, and I shared a room with Kiran in the hostel during board exam season. Kiran, sixteen, was the most organised person I've ever seen.
On the wall above his desk he taped a chart: every subject split into chapters, each with a date and a colour. Hard chapters in the morning, easy revision at night. His phone went into my cupboard from six to nine every evening. "Lock it, and don't give it back even if I beg," he said.
Two days before physics, he panicked because he couldn't solve a numerical. He stopped, walked around the block, came back and did five past papers, timing each one.
In the exam hall, he started with the section he found easiest. I don't know if he felt calm inside, but he looked it. I copied his chart for the next term.

qa.q: Where did Kiran's phone go from six to nine every evening?
qa.a: His phone went into Pranav's cupboard.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling two days before physics?
qa.a: Kiran felt panicked and anxious when he couldn't solve a numerical so close to the exam.

qa.q: What exam strategies could another student learn from Kiran?
qa.a: Plan revision by chapter and date, keep the phone away during study hours, practise timed past papers, and start the exam with the easiest section.

qa.q: How does Pranav see Kiran's way of studying?
qa.a: Pranav admires it and finds it so useful that he copies Kiran's chart for the next term.

grounding: Shows a teenager planning revision, blocking distraction and managing nerves before a high-stakes exam.
